scores.evidence: Truly zero write pause is only possible if the application was built for it. Plan for near-zero
scores.rationale: Accurate on single write authority, CDC, reverse replication and DNS TTL; minor imprecision such as DNS-flip reliance and no mention of sequence/identity handling in reverse replication.

scores.evidence: Switch the database that accepts bookings in one step. Most systems need a pause in new bookings of seconds to a few minutes.
scores.rationale: Honestly reinterprets zero downtime as near-zero with read-only continuity and covers core needs, but is thin on specifics like cost and exclusions.

scores.evidence: One database accepts bookings at a time; freeze bookings at the switch
scores.rationale: Consistent single-writer design with reverse replication and rollback, though the optional phasing and the cutover table's read-only step are lightly connected.

scores.evidence: at least two complete practice cutovers and rollbacks in a staging copy, each timed.
scores.rationale: Validation targets main risks (shadow HL7, load test, failure tests, rehearsals, lag thresholds) with checkable criteria, but little post-launch validation and some thresholds are unjustified.

scores.evidence: I don't have details about your system, so this plan uses common assumptions.
scores.rationale: States assumptions and asks questions, but doesn't say how specific design parts change if the assumptions are wrong beyond vendor and shared-resource notes.

scores.evidence: Watch for duplicates. Reminders and outbound messages must not fire from both environments.
scores.rationale: Covers double-booking, duplicate reminders, hidden integrations, AZ and link loss, rollback, but little on data corruption, adversarial input, or partial failure mid-cutover.

scores.evidence: Support period of 2–4 weeks: extra staff on hand and daily check-ins with clinic managers.
scores.rationale: Covers rollback, hypercare and monitoring in passing, but lacks specific health signals, ownership and incident response.

scores.evidence: Typical timeline: 4–6 months for a mid-size hospital
scores.rationale: Cost is essentially unaddressed beyond a timeline; only running on-prem for 30–90 days is implied as overlap cost.

scores.evidence: Time-box the rollback decision, for example within 72 hours. After that, problems are fixed forward in the cloud.
scores.rationale: Reverse replication, read-only-first, lift-and-shift without redesign, and IaC isolate commitments; vendor lock-in and key/ID choices not examined.

scores.evidence: move the app as-is with a managed database. Don't redesign the app as part of this migration; that adds risk.
scores.rationale: Lean phased design; every element is justified and no speculative components.

scores.evidence: T+3–5 min | Point the app, load balancer and interface engine to the cloud; start reverse replication
scores.rationale: Ordered phases with a timed cutover runbook and go/no-go gates; remains generic on tooling choices and team roles.

checklist.evidence: Sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with the cloud provider (HIPAA, or your local equivalent). Use only services the provider lists as eligible
Map every integration. ... EHR/ADT feeds and HL7 SIU scheduling messages; Interface engine (Mirth, Rhapsody, Cloverleaf)
Check continuously: row counts, checksums on key tables (appointments, slots, resources, patients), and replication lag.
One database accepts bookings at a time; freeze bookings at the switch
Prepare reverse replication (cloud back to on-prem). ... at least two complete practice cutovers and rollbacks
a dedicated link (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute or Interconnect) plus a backup VPN
run across multiple availability zones, with backups, monitoring, and central logging.
single sign-on or AD integration so staff log in exactly as they do now.
Load testing at 1.5–2× your Monday-morning peak ... Send copies of HL7 traffic to the cloud environment in shadow mode.
Agree a change freeze around cutover ... Support period of 2–4 weeks: extra staff on hand
If it's a vendor product ... confirm early that the vendor supports your cloud and approach.

traps.evidence: Continuous change capture to keep the cloud copy current
That rules out simply running two live copies side by side.
Use only services the provider lists as eligible for patient data.
Map every integration. This is usually where the risk is
Don't redesign the app as part of this migration; that adds risk.

note: Sound, proportionate single-writer CDC migration with reverse replication and rehearsed rollback; weak on cost, operations detail, and the specifics of HIPAA, DR targets and break-glass access.
